questions.question: How do you handle errors end-to-end in a WebFlux application?
questions.title: WebFlux Error Handling: Operators, Controllers, Global Handlers
questions.direct_answer: WebFlux error handling layers from inside-out: **operator-level** (`onErrorResume`, `onErrorReturn`, `onErrorMap`, `retryWhen`, `timeout`) handles recoverable errors inside the reactive chain; **controller-level** `@ExceptionHandler` catches signals for one controller; **global** `@RestControllerAdvice` maps domain exceptions to HTTP responses consistently; and **`WebExceptionHandler`** is the last-line catch for filter, routing, and security errors. Status mapping uses `ResponseStatusException` or RFC 7807 `ProblemDetail`. Critical gotchas: errors in Reactor are signals — `try/catch` doesn't catch them; `onErrorContinue` silently swallows bugs; request context survives only through Reactor `Context` or the Micrometer Context Propagation bridge.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical reactive error handling, layered approach, HTTP mapping, observability, and Reactor Context for MDC
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing blocking try/catch with reactive chains; using onErrorContinue blindly; losing request context across threads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss ProblemDetail RFC 7807, Reactor Context for MDC, retry with jitter and idempotency, exception hierarchy design, and per-endpoint error budgets

sections.title: Errors as Signals — The Reactive Mindset
sections.content:
Reactive error handling is fundamentally different from blocking Java. **In Reactor, an error is a signal that terminates the sequence** — not a thrown exception that bubbles up the call stack. You handle it via operators inside the chain, by catching boundary exceptions, or by mapping it to a user-facing HTTP error.

**Four layers of defense**, from innermost to outermost:

- **Operator-level** — recoverable / expected errors handled inside the reactive chain (`onErrorResume`, `retryWhen`, `timeout`)
- **Controller-level** — `@ExceptionHandler` methods on a specific `@RestController`
- **Global** — `@RestControllerAdvice` with `@ExceptionHandler` methods that apply across controllers
- **Framework-level** — a custom `WebExceptionHandler` bean for anything earlier layers missed (filter errors, routing, security)

**Rules of thumb:**
- Recoverable / expected errors (fallback value, retry, alternative source) → operator-level
- Unrecoverable / domain errors mapped to a specific HTTP status → global advice
- Truly unexpected → framework-level catches it and returns a generic 5xx

Response format should follow **RFC 7807 Problem Details** (`application/problem+json`) for consistent client experience, with a `traceId` so users can report failures and on-call can find logs.

sections.title: How an onError Signal Propagates
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    req[HTTP Request] --> ctl["Controller method (Mono / Flux)"]
    ctl --> chain["Reactor chain: map / flatMap / etc"]
    chain -->|onNext / onComplete| ok["200 / 201 success"]
    chain -->|onError signal| op["Operator handlers: onErrorResume / retry / timeout"]
    op -->|recovered| ok
    op -->|propagated| ctlEx["Controller @ExceptionHandler"]
    ctlEx -->|no match| advice["@RestControllerAdvice global"]
    advice -->|no match| weh["WebExceptionHandler last line"]
    weh --> err["5xx with ProblemDetail"]
    advice --> err
    ctlEx --> err
```

sections.title: Operator-Level Error Handling
sections.content:
Handle errors inside the reactive chain to recover, fall back, or transform.

**Fallback value**
- Use `onErrorReturn` to substitute a default when an error occurs
- Best for cheap, safe defaults that don't need branching

```java
productRepo.findById(id)
    .onErrorReturn(Product.unavailable(id));
```

**Fallback publisher**
- Use `onErrorResume` when the recovery itself is an async call
- Branch on exception type for fine-grained recovery

```java
productRepo.findById(id)
    .onErrorResume(e -> {
        if (e instanceof DataAccessException)
            return cacheClient.getProduct(id);
        return Mono.error(e);
    });
```

**Type-specific handling**
- Filter by exception class for clarity

```java
.onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just(ProductDto.deferred(id)))
.onErrorResume(NotFoundException.class, e -> Mono.empty())
```

**Mapping / translating exceptions**
- `onErrorMap` wraps a low-level exception in a domain one
- Keeps error contract clean across layer boundaries

```java
.onErrorMap(SQLException.class, e -> new DatabaseException("DB failed", e))
```

**Retry with backoff and jitter**
- Use `Retry.backoff` with `maxBackoff` and a filter
- Always restrict to known-retryable exceptions

```java
webClient.get().uri("/price").retrieve().bodyToMono(Price.class)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .retryWhen(Retry
        .backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200))
        .maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .filter(this::isRetryable)
        .onRetryExhaustedThrow((spec, sig) -> sig.failure()));
```

**Don't retry:**
- 4xx responses (will always fail the same way)
- Non-idempotent operations without dedup / idempotency key
- Timeouts on writes (the request may have succeeded; only the response was lost)

**Timeout — every outbound call needs one**

```java
.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3), Mono.just(Fallback.value()))
```

**`onErrorContinue` — rare and risky**
- Skips errored items and continues upstream
- Not all operators respect it consistently
- Can mask bugs by silently dropping items
- The Reactor docs explicitly discourage general use
- Prefer per-item handling inside `flatMap`

```java
items.flatMap(item ->
    processItem(item)
        .onErrorResume(e -> {
            log.warn("failed item {}", item, e);
            return Mono.empty();
        }));
```

**Logging without transforming**

```java
.doOnError(e -> log.error("fetch failed", e))
```

**Context for error logs (request ID, user, tenant)**
- Reactor `Context` survives across operator boundaries
- Spring Boot 3.x bridges it to MDC via Micrometer Context Propagation

```java
.doOnError(e -> Mono.deferContextual(ctx ->
    Mono.fromRunnable(() ->
        log.error("fetch failed for tenant {}", ctx.get("tenant"), e))));
```

sections.title: Controller and Global Error Handling
Framework-Level WebExceptionHandler and Security
Common Pitfalls and Production Best Practices
sections.content:
**When operator-level handling helps:**
- Recovery is cheap, deterministic, and local (cache fallback, default value)
- You want retry with backoff for a known transient failure
- The chain has multiple stages and one of them needs special treatment

**When global advice is the right home:**
- Mapping a domain exception to an HTTP status across many controllers
- Producing a consistent `ProblemDetail` envelope
- Centralized validation error formatting

**When WebExceptionHandler matters:**
- Filter / security / routing errors that never reach a controller
- Last-line guarantee that the client gets a structured response

**Pitfalls to avoid:**
- **`try/catch` around reactive calls** — `productRepo.findById(id)` returns a `Mono` immediately; the error happens later inside the chain and is never caught
- **`.block()` in reactive code** — defeats non-blocking; risks deadlock on event-loop threads
- **Swallowing errors silently** — `onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty())` without logging or metric = invisible failures
- **`onErrorContinue` misuse** — looks convenient but is inconsistent across operators; prefer per-item `flatMap(...).onErrorResume`
- **Losing context** — MDC and tenant info are ThreadLocal in blocking world; in reactive use Reactor `Context` plus Micrometer Context Propagation
- **No timeout on outbound calls** — every `WebClient` / `WebSocketClient` / external call needs explicit `timeout()`
- **Retrying non-idempotent writes** — without an idempotency key you risk duplicate orders / payments
- **Bad error messages** — exposing stack traces, internal paths, DB error text leaks information; return generic for 5xx, detailed for 4xx validation
- **No correlation ID** — every error response should include a trace ID the user can quote and on-call can search for
- **Status code mismatches** — invalid input is 400, missing resource is 404, auth failure is 401 vs 403, business rule violation is 409 / 422

**Recommended exception hierarchy:**

```
BaseAppException (abstract)
  NotFoundException        -> 404
  ValidationException      -> 400
  AuthorizationException   -> 403
  UpstreamException        -> 502
  BusinessRuleException    -> 409 or 422
```

Global advice maps each branch to a `ProblemDetail` with consistent fields (`traceId`, `timestamp`, `errorCode`).

**Observability integration:**
- Log with error class, code, traceId, route, user / tenant
- Increment counter `errors.total{class="NotFound", endpoint="/orders"}`
- `span.recordException(ex); span.setStatus(ERROR)` via OpenTelemetry
- Alert on error-rate SLO burn, not raw counts

**Testing error paths:**

```java
webTestClient.get().uri("/orders/missing")
    .exchange()
    .expectStatus().isNotFound()
    .expectBody(ProblemDetail.class)
    .value(pd -> assertThat(pd.getDetail()).contains("not found"));
```

```java
StepVerifier.create(myMono)
    .expectErrorMatches(t -> t instanceof MyException
        && t.getMessage().contains("specific"))
    .verify();
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Errors are signals** in Reactor — handle via operators, not try/catch
- **Layer handling** — operator → controller `@ExceptionHandler` → `@RestControllerAdvice` → `WebExceptionHandler`
- **`onErrorResume` / `onErrorReturn` / `onErrorMap`** cover fallback publisher, fallback value, and translation
- **`retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...))`** with jitter and exception filter is the standard retry pattern
- **Always `timeout()`** on outbound calls; default is dangerous
- **`onErrorContinue` is risky** — prefer per-item `flatMap(...).onErrorResume`
- **`ProblemDetail` (RFC 7807)** is the modern response format, built into Spring 6
- **Preserve context** with Reactor `Context` plus Micrometer Context Propagation
- **Map domain exceptions to HTTP status** consistently in `@RestControllerAdvice`
- **Don't leak internals** — generic messages for 5xx, detailed for 4xx validation
- **Trace IDs in every error response**; alert on error-rate SLO burn

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
WebFlux error handling layers from inside-out: operator-level, controller-level, global advice, framework-level.

**The four layers**

*Operator-level:*
- `onErrorResume`, `onErrorReturn`, `onErrorMap` for recovery and translation
- `retryWhen` with backoff for transient failures
- `timeout` on every outbound call

*Controller-level:*
- `@ExceptionHandler` on a specific controller

*Global:*
- `@RestControllerAdvice` mapping domain exceptions to HTTP
- One place for consistent `ProblemDetail` responses

*Framework-level:*
- `WebExceptionHandler` for filter, routing, security errors
- Last line of defense

**Rules of thumb**
- Recoverable / expected → operator-level
- Domain → HTTP mapping → global advice
- Truly unexpected → framework-level returns generic 5xx

**Critical things to mention**
- Errors in Reactor are signals, not thrown exceptions; `try/catch` doesn't catch them
- `.block()` in reactive code defeats non-blocking and risks deadlock
- Never swallow errors silently — at minimum log or count them
- `onErrorContinue` is inconsistent across operators; prefer per-item `flatMap` plus `onErrorResume`
- Reactor `Context` plus Micrometer Context Propagation keeps MDC and trace IDs across thread hops
- Every outbound call needs an explicit timeout — defaults are too long or absent
- Don't retry 4xx, don't retry non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key

**HTTP error contract**
- RFC 7807 `ProblemDetail` is the modern standard, built into Spring 6
- Content-Type `application/problem+json`
- Fields: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`, plus custom properties
- Always include a trace ID so users can report and on-call can search

**Strategic answer**
- Operator-level for recovery; global advice for HTTP mapping; framework-level for last-line
- Errors are first-class citizens, not afterthoughts
- Consistent exception hierarchy + `ProblemDetail` = clean error contract
- Log with context, alert on rates, never expose internals to users

questions.question: How do you compose retry, timeout, and circuit breaker for reactive WebClient calls?
questions.title: Reactive Resilience — Retry, Timeout, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead
questions.direct_answer: Resilience for outbound `WebClient` calls layers four primitives: **`timeout`** bounds latency (always set per call), **`retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...))`** with jitter and an exception filter retries idempotent transient failures, **circuit breaker** (Resilience4j reactive) stops hammering a degraded upstream, and **bulkhead** isolates concurrency per downstream so one slow service can't drain capacity. Order matters in the operator chain — `timeout` innermost, then `retry`, then circuit breaker outermost — so retries respect timeout and the breaker counts retried failures correctly. Never retry non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key, and never retry 4xx.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate composes resilience primitives correctly, understands operator order, idempotency, and Resilience4j reactive integration
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Retrying non-idempotent writes; placing timeout outside retry; using fixed-delay retries; no jitter; no exception filter; no fallback
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss operator order rationale, jittered backoff, idempotency keys, hedged requests, bulkheads per downstream, and circuit breaker tuning by SLO

sections.title: Why Layered Resilience
sections.content:
A WebFlux service that calls upstreams will eventually face slow, flaky, or degraded dependencies. **Timeouts**, **retries**, **circuit breakers**, and **bulkheads** each address a different failure mode. Composing them correctly turns transient upstream issues into recoverable blips instead of cascading outages.

**The four primitives:**
- **Timeout** — bounds per-call latency; without it a single hung upstream eats all your concurrency
- **Retry with backoff and jitter** — retries idempotent transient failures (5xx, network blips) with growing waits
- **Circuit breaker** — stops hammering a clearly-broken upstream and short-circuits to a fallback
- **Bulkhead** — isolates concurrency per downstream so one slow service can't starve others

**Order matters in the operator chain**
- `timeout` innermost (per-attempt bound)
- `retryWhen` next (each retry respects the timeout)
- circuit breaker outermost (counts the final outcome of the retry sequence)
- fallback after the breaker

sections.title: Timeout — the Non-Negotiable Baseline
sections.content:
**Per-call timeout on every outbound `WebClient`**
- Default Reactor Netty connect / response timeouts are too generous or absent
- Set a connection timeout, a response timeout, and a per-request `.timeout(Duration)` for safety

```java
HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.create()
    .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 2_000)
    .responseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
    .doOnConnected(conn -> conn
        .addHandlerLast(new ReadTimeoutHandler(3))
        .addHandlerLast(new WriteTimeoutHandler(3)));

WebClient paymentClient = WebClient.builder()
    .baseUrl("https://payments.internal")
    .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(httpClient))
    .build();

Mono<PaymentResult> charge(Charge c) {
    return paymentClient.post().uri("/charge")
        .bodyValue(c)
        .retrieve()
        .bodyToMono(PaymentResult.class)
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3));
}
```

**Tuning rule**
- Per-call timeout < your service's own SLO; otherwise upstream slowness becomes your slowness
- Pick from p99 + buffer of upstream, not p50

sections.title: Retry — Backoff, Jitter, and Filters
Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead with Resilience4j
sections.content:
**Resilience4j Reactor integration**
- `CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb)` wraps a `Mono` / `Flux`
- `BulkheadOperator.of(bh)` limits concurrent in-flight calls
- Apply via `.transformDeferred(...)` for per-subscription state

```yaml
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payments:
        slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 50
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 20
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 10s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      payments:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 25
        maxWaitDuration: 0ms
```

```java
@Service
class PaymentService {
    private final WebClient paymentClient;
    private final CircuitBreaker breaker;
    private final Bulkhead bulkhead;

    PaymentService(WebClient paymentClient,
                   CircuitBreakerRegistry cbRegistry,
                   BulkheadRegistry bhRegistry) {
        this.paymentClient = paymentClient;
        this.breaker = cbRegistry.circuitBreaker("payments");
        this.bulkhead = bhRegistry.bulkhead("payments");
    }

    Mono<PaymentResult> charge(Charge c) {
        return paymentClient.post().uri("/charge")
            .bodyValue(c)
            .retrieve()
            .bodyToMono(PaymentResult.class)
            .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3))
            .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200))
                .maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
                .jitter(0.5)
                .filter(this::isRetryable))
            .transformDeferred(BulkheadOperator.of(bulkhead))
            .transformDeferred(CircuitBreakerOperator.of(breaker))
            .onErrorResume(CallNotPermittedException.class,
                ex -> Mono.just(PaymentResult.fallback(c.id())));
    }
}
```

**Why this order**
- `timeout` innermost — bounds each attempt
- `retryWhen` next — each retry attempt respects the timeout
- `BulkheadOperator` — limits in-flight concurrency for this dependency
- `CircuitBreakerOperator` — sees the final outcome of the (timeout + retry) sequence; trips when too many fail
- `onErrorResume(CallNotPermittedException)` — the breaker's open state surfaces here; return a degraded but valid response

sections.title: When to Use Each Primitive
sections.content:
Each primitive solves a different problem. Combine them — don't pick one.

| Primitive | Problem It Solves | When To Use | Pitfall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Timeout | Hung upstreams eat concurrency | Every outbound call, no exception | Set too high — cascades latency |
| Retry + jitter | Transient blips (network, 5xx) | Idempotent reads; writes with idempotency key | Retrying 4xx or unsafe writes |
| Circuit breaker | Sustained upstream failure / brownout | Critical dependencies with fallback | Too small a window — false trips |
| Bulkhead | One slow upstream starves others | Multiple distinct downstreams | Too small — drops legitimate load |

sections.title: Composition Order, Hedging, and Pitfalls
sections.content:
**When layered resilience helps:**
- Critical user-facing flows that depend on flaky internal services
- Dependencies with known SLO and failure characteristics
- Multi-tenant systems where one tenant's traffic shouldn't degrade others
- Long-tail latency: hedged requests against multiple replicas

**When layered resilience hurts:**
- Over-retrying amplifies upstream outages (retry storms)
- A breaker without a fallback turns a slow failure into a fast failure
- Bulkheads sized too small drop legitimate spikes
- Compounding timeouts (3s outer, 3s retry, 3 retries = up to ~12s) breaks SLOs

**Watch for — common pitfalls:**
- **Wrong operator order** — `timeout` outside `retry` means retries don't respect per-attempt latency
- **No jitter** — synchronized retries pile on the upstream during recovery
- **Retrying writes without idempotency** — duplicate orders, double-charges
- **Retrying 4xx** — wastes budget and capacity
- **Long open-state duration** with no graceful degradation — users see errors longer than necessary
- **Shared circuit breaker across endpoints** — one bad endpoint trips all
- **No metrics** — `resilience4j` exposes Micrometer metrics; alert on open-state and rejection rates
- **Forgetting fallbacks** — `onErrorResume(CallNotPermittedException...)` must produce a usable degraded response

**Hedged requests for tail-latency reduction**
- Fire a duplicate request after a short delay; take whichever returns first
- Costs ~5 percent extra calls; cuts p99 dramatically

```java
Mono<PaymentResult> hedged = Mono.firstWithSignal(
    charge(c),
    charge(c).delaySubscription(Duration.ofMillis(150))
);
```

**Per-downstream bulkhead, not per-call**
- One bulkhead per logical dependency (payments, search, recommendations)
- Sizing rule: `maxConcurrent ~= target_qps * p99_latency_seconds`

**Strategic guidance:**
- Every outbound call: timeout + jittered retry + circuit breaker + fallback
- Use idempotency keys for any retried write
- Tune timeouts from upstream p99 + buffer, not from p50
- Tune circuit breaker by SLO burn rate, not arbitrary thresholds
- Bulkhead per downstream, sized by target qps × latency
- Always expose Micrometer metrics; alert on open-state and rejection counts

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Timeout** is mandatory on every outbound call; without it one hung upstream eats your concurrency
- **Retry with backoff and jitter** for transient errors only; filter exceptions explicitly
- **Never retry 4xx**, and never retry non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key
- **Circuit breaker** stops hammering a clearly-degraded upstream; pair with a fallback
- **Bulkhead** isolates concurrency per downstream so one slow service can't starve others
- **Operator order** — timeout innermost, retry next, breaker outermost; the breaker sees final outcomes
- **Hedged requests** cut p99 by firing a duplicate after a short delay; `Mono.firstWithSignal`
- **Resilience4j** exposes reactor operators (`CircuitBreakerOperator`, `BulkheadOperator`) and Micrometer metrics
- **Tune from SLO** — timeouts from upstream p99, breaker from error budget burn rate
- **Always provide a fallback** for `CallNotPermittedException` so users get a degraded but valid response

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Resilience for outbound WebClient calls layers four primitives — timeout, retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead — each solving a different failure mode.

**The four primitives**
- Timeout — bounds per-call latency; mandatory
- Retry with backoff and jitter — idempotent transient failures only
- Circuit breaker — stops hammering a degraded upstream
- Bulkhead — isolates concurrency per downstream

**Operator order**
- `timeout` innermost — bounds each attempt
- `retryWhen` next — each retry respects the timeout
- `BulkheadOperator` — caps in-flight concurrency
- `CircuitBreakerOperator` outermost — sees the final outcome
- `onErrorResume(CallNotPermittedException)` — fallback on open breaker

**Retry rules**
- Never retry 4xx
- Never retry non-idempotent writes without an idempotency key
- Always include jitter — synchronized retries amplify outages
- Cap attempts (3 typical) and total budget
- Filter exceptions explicitly — retry only 502 / 503 / 504 / TimeoutException

**Resilience4j**
- `CircuitBreakerOperator.of(cb)` and `BulkheadOperator.of(bh)` via `.transformDeferred`
- Configure in YAML — sliding window, failure threshold, wait duration, half-open calls
- Exposes Micrometer metrics — alert on open-state and rejection rates

**Hedged requests**
- `Mono.firstWithSignal(call, call.delaySubscription(150ms))`
- ~5 percent extra calls; cuts p99 dramatically

**Tuning rules**
- Timeout from upstream p99 + buffer, not p50
- Per-call timeout < your own SLO
- Bulkhead size ~= target qps × p99 latency
- Circuit breaker tuned by SLO burn rate, not arbitrary thresholds

**Common pitfalls**
- Wrong operator order — timeout outside retry breaks per-attempt bounds
- No jitter — retry storms
- Retrying writes without idempotency keys — duplicates
- Shared breaker across endpoints — one bad endpoint trips all
- No fallback — slow failure becomes fast failure with no value

**Strategic answer**
- Every outbound call: timeout + jittered retry + breaker + fallback
- Idempotency keys for any retried write
- Bulkhead per downstream
- Metrics and alerts on rejection / open-state
- Tune from observed p99 and SLO burn, not guesses
